specPoints.text: understand the mechanisms of the nucleophilic substitution reactions between primary halogenoalkanes and: i aqueous potassium hydroxide ii ammonia S N 1 and S N 2 substitution mechanisms will be tested in Unit 4.

primer.text: Four nucleophiles, four destinations: hydroxide to alcohols in aqueous warmth, cyanide to chain-extended nitriles under reflux, ammonia to primary amines under pressure, and ethanolic hydroxide to alkenes by elimination. This note steers the conditions and counts the carbons each route leaves behind.

lessons.title: Nucleophiles and the alcohol route
lessons.opening: The hydroxide ion is chemistry's electron-rich hand: it donates a pair into the halogenoalkane's d+ carbon and walks off with the halogen's job. Warm aqueous alkali - never ethanolic - turns halogenoalkanes into alcohols by hydrolysis.
keyPoints: A nucleophile carries electron richness and donates an electron pair, drawn toward positive centres.
Aqueous NaOH or KOH (with ethanol co-solvent) warms with the halogenoalkane to form an alcohol.
Water as the primary solvent is essential: ethanolic conditions would give elimination instead.
The reaction is hydrolysis; its rate depends on the C-X bond, strongest for C-F and weakest for C-I.

low.restatement: Hydroxide donates a lone pair to the polarised carbon, replacing the halogen; aqueous conditions keep the route on substitution, warm conditions keep it moving at all.
low.analogy: A magnet-handed guest (OH-) swaps places with the house's current occupant (halogen) at the carbon's front door.
low.examPointer: Quote the solvent rule: aqueous gives the alcohol, ethanolic gives the alkene - the examiner's favourite condition trap.

medium.restatement: Hydroxide out-nucleophiles water because its full negative charge attacks where water only offers a partial negative oxygen; hence aqueous alkali reacts far faster than water alone. Bond enthalpy ranks the substrate rates from the strongest C-F down through C-Cl and C-Br to the weakest C-I.
medium.analogy: A full wallet buys faster than partial credit: OH- pays in full charge, water only in partial charge.
medium.examPointer: Name the reaction hydrolysis and rank fluoroalkanes (unreactive) against iodoalkanes (fastest) when asked about rates.

check.stem: A nucleophile is defined as

options.text: An electron-rich species able to give away a pair of electrons
options.explanation: Attraction to positive centres follows from that richness.
That is the electrophile.

options.text: Any species with a full negative charge
options.explanation: Definition runs on electron-pair donation, not charge alone.
Nucleophiles are consumed as reactants.

check.stem: Which conditions convert a halogenoalkane to an alcohol?

options.explanation: Aqueous OH- with gentle warming hydrolyses the C-X bond to the alcohol.
Ethanolic conditions eliminate to the alkene instead.
Ammonia gives amines, and only under ethanolic pressure-heating.
That reagent belongs to halide tests, not alcohol synthesis.

check.stem: Why must water be the primary solvent for the alcohol route?

options.text: Ethanolic conditions steer the reaction to elimination, forming an alkene
options.explanation: Solvent choice selects the pathway: aqueous substitution versus ethanolic elimination.
No freezing effect is involved.
Water is the solvent medium, not a catalyst.

options.text: The alcohol dissolves only in water
options.explanation: Solubility of the product is not the governing reason.

check.stem: The hydroxide ion beats water as a nucleophile because

options.text: It carries a full negative charge where water's oxygen carries only partial charge
options.explanation: Full charge means stronger electron-pair donation and faster attack.

options.text: It is lighter and moves faster
options.explanation: Mass is not the deciding factor.

options.text: It is larger and more visible
options.explanation: Size and visibility are irrelevant.

options.text: Water is not a nucleophile at all
options.explanation: Water is a weak nucleophile - it eventually substitutes.

check.stem: Rank the halogenoalkanes by rate of hydrolysis with aqueous OH-:

options.text: Iodoalkane fastest, then bromo, then chloro, fluoro unreactive
options.explanation: Weakest C-X bond (C-I) breaks fastest; C-F is too strong to react.
Electronegativity is outweighed by bond enthalpy.

options.text: Chloro fastest, since C-Cl is most polar
options.explanation: Polarity suggests but bond strength decides.

options.text: All equal rates, as each carries one halogen
options.explanation: The C-X bond strength varies hugely down the group.

check.stem: Define the term nucleophile.
check.modelAnswer: A species rich in electrons that gives a pair away to an electron-deficient centre.

check.stem: State the conditions and product for the alcohol route.
check.modelAnswer: Warm aqueous NaOH or KOH (ethanol as co-solvent) gives the alcohol by hydrolysis.

check.stem: Explain why fluoroalkanes do not undergo the hydroxide substitution at all.
check.modelAnswer: The C-F bond is the strongest carbon-halogen bond, so hydroxide cannot break it under these conditions.

check.stem: A chemist accidentally uses pure ethanol as solvent with NaOH instead of aqueous alkali. Predict the organic product and name the reaction class.
check.modelAnswer: An alkene forms by elimination rather than the intended alcohol; the reaction class switches from nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) to elimination.

lessons.title: The nitrile route: chain extension with cyanide
lessons.opening: Cyanide is the carbon accountant's favourite nucleophile: it substitutes the halogen and leaves one extra carbon behind. Bromoethane heated under reflux with ethanolic KCN emerges as propanenitrile - two carbons in, three carbons out.
keyPoints: The nucleophile in the nitrile route is the cyanide ion, CN-.
An ethanolic solution of KCN is heated under reflux with the halogenoalkane.
Bromoethane plus ethanolic KCN under reflux forms propanenitrile.
The substitution extends the carbon chain by one carbon, a synthetic tool for building larger molecules.

low.restatement: Cyanide's carbon lands on the substrate's d+ carbon; the extra carbon in CN- means the nitrile product carries one more carbon than the starting halogenoalkane.
low.analogy: A one-brick extension bolted onto a house: CN- donates its carbon brick and stays as the roof (the nitrile group).
low.examPointer: State the chain-extension consequence explicitly - it is the route's synthetic selling point and a standing exam question.

medium.restatement: Reflux with ethanolic KCN supplies both the nucleophile and the heat; the incoming nitrile carbon becomes carbon 1 of the -C#N group, so counting carbons through the nitrile carbon gives the +1 product.
medium.analogy: The cyanide ion arrives holding a spare carbon in each hand; one hand bonds to the substrate, the other holds the nitrogen cap.
medium.examPointer: Count carbons in the product name: propanenitrile from bromoethane - the nitrile carbon itself is included in the count.

check.stem: The nucleophile in the nitrile-forming reaction is

options.explanation: Cyanide donates its carbon lone pair to the halogenoalkane.
Hydroxide gives alcohols, not nitriles.
Ammonia gives amines.
The halide departs; it does not attack.

check.stem: The conditions for forming a nitrile are

options.explanation: Reflux heat with ethanolic cyanide drives the substitution.
The standard route specifies ethanol and reflux.
That combination gives elimination to the alkene.
Ammonia's route gives primary amines.

check.stem: Bromoethane reacting with ethanolic KCN gives propanenitrile because

options.text: The cyanide ion contributes its own carbon, extending the chain from two to three
options.explanation: C2 substrate plus the C of CN- gives a C3 nitrile.

options.text: The bromine is replaced by three carbons
options.explanation: Only one carbon is added per substitution.
No dimerisation occurs.

options.text: The ethanol solvent adds a carbon
options.explanation: The solvent does not enter the product.

check.stem: A chemist wants a compound with one more carbon than the best available starting material. The useful reaction is

options.text: Halogenoalkane with ethanolic KCN under reflux
options.explanation: Cyanide substitution adds exactly one carbon.
That route keeps the carbon count unchanged.
Amines also keep the substrate's carbon count.
Water's slow hydrolysis adds no carbon.

check.stem: In propanenitrile formed from bromoethane, the nitrile carbon counts as

options.explanation: Nitrile carbon is included in the parent count.

options.text: A side group outside the chain count
options.explanation: The -C#N carbon is part of the counted chain.
It is the very carbon cyanide donated.
The nitrile carbon carries the highest priority and is numbered 1.

check.stem: State the product class and conditions for the cyanide route.
check.modelAnswer: A nitrile forms when the halogenoalkane is heated under reflux with ethanolic KCN.

check.stem: State the synthetic value of the cyanide substitution.
check.modelAnswer: It extends the carbon chain by one carbon, enabling synthesis of larger molecules from smaller starting materials.

check.stem: Explain why the cyanide ion is nucleophilic.
check.modelAnswer: Cyanide carries a full negative charge with a lone pair on its carbon, so it donates an electron pair into the halogenoalkane's electron-poor carbon.

check.stem: Predict the organic product of 1-chloropropane with ethanolic KCN under reflux, and give its carbon count.
check.modelAnswer: Butanenitrile: the C3 chain gains cyanide's carbon to give a four-carbon nitrile (the nitrile carbon counted as C1).

lessons.title: The amine route: ammonia under pressure
sourceHeadings: Formation of primary amines by reaction with ammonia
lessons.opening: Ammonia joins the nucleophile club with its lone pair, and excess ammonia under ethanolic pressure-heating converts primary halogenoalkanes into primary amines. Excess matters: the amine product is itself reactive, and only surplus NH3 suppresses its further substitution.
keyPoints: The nucleophile in the amine route is the ammonia molecule, NH3.
Excess ammonia in ethanol, warmed under pressure, reacts with a primary halogenoalkane.
The product is a primary amine; bromoethane gives ethylamine.
Excess ammonia suppresses further substitution because the amine product is more reactive than ammonia.

low.restatement: Ammonia's lone pair attacks the d+ carbon, swapping the halogen for NH2; flooding the vessel with excess NH3 keeps the newly formed amine from attacking another substrate molecule.
low.analogy: A queue where the formed product is shooed away by a crowd of fresh ammonia molecules before it can bite again.
low.examPointer: Quote both conditions (excess, ethanolic, pressure, heat) and the 'more reactive product' reason - all appear in mark schemes.

medium.restatement: The substitution installs NH2 where the halogen sat, so the carbon count is unchanged; primary substrates keep the amine primary. Pressure keeps ammonia, a gas, in the reacting solution.
medium.analogy: The ammonia hands its nitrogen arm to the carbon skeleton; the skeleton's length and degree stay exactly as they were.
medium.examPointer: Name the product class primary amine and check the carbon count is conserved - a common slip is inventing chain growth here.

check.stem: The nucleophile in primary amine synthesis is

options.explanation: Ammonia's lone pair performs the substitution.
The route uses ammonia molecules.
NH4+ has no lone pair to donate.
The halide leaves; it does not attack.

check.stem: Excess ammonia is used because

options.text: The amine product is more reactive than ammonia and could undergo further substitution
options.explanation: Flooding with NH3 keeps collisions on ammonia rather than the amine.

options.text: Ammonia is expensive and must be recovered
options.explanation: Excess implies using more, not saving.
Pressure is applied regardless.
No neutralisation role is assigned to excess NH3.

check.stem: Bromoethane with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure and heat gives

options.explanation: NH2 replaces Br on the two-carbon chain.
That is the cyanide route's product.
Further substitution is suppressed by the excess ammonia.
That is the aqueous alkali route.

check.stem: Why must the halogenoalkane be primary for this route as taught?

options.text: The taught substitution installs NH2 on a primary carbon to give a primary amine
options.explanation: The route as specified targets primary halogenoalkanes.

options.text: Secondary halogenoalkanes are too reactive to store
options.explanation: Storage stability is not the reason.

options.text: Ammonia cannot attack secondary carbons at all
options.explanation: The specification simply teaches the primary route.
No such hazard is the stated reason.

check.stem: Heating under pressure in the amine route serves to

options.text: Keep gaseous ammonia dissolved in the reacting ethanolic solution while warming the reaction
options.explanation: Pressure retains NH3 so the nucleophile stays available.

options.text: Raise the boiling point of the amine
options.explanation: The amine's properties are irrelevant.
Conditions are not catalysts.
No such conversion is part of the route.

check.stem: State the conditions for the amine route.
check.modelAnswer: Excess ethanolic ammonia, heated under pressure, with a primary halogenoalkane.

check.stem: Name the organic product class and one example.
check.modelAnswer: Primary amine; for example ethylamine from bromoethane.

check.stem: Explain why the amine product could cause further substitution if ammonia were not in excess.
check.modelAnswer: The amine's nitrogen still carries a lone pair, making it a nucleophile able to attack remaining halogenoalkane; excess ammonia out-competes it.

check.stem: 1-bromopropane reacts with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure. Name the product and state its carbon count.
check.modelAnswer: Propylamine (a primary amine) with three carbons - the substitution conserves the chain length.

lessons.title: The alkene route: elimination with ethanolic hydroxide
lessons.opening: Same reagent, different solvent, opposite outcome: hot ethanolic NaOH rips HX out of the halogenoalkane, breaking the C-X bond heterolytically and leaving a double bond. Bromoethane becomes ethene, the solvent having flipped substitution into elimination.
keyPoints: Halogenoalkanes heated with ethanolic sodium hydroxide undergo elimination.
The C-X bond breaks heterolytically, forming an X- ion and an alkene.
Bromoethane with hot ethanolic NaOH forms ethene.
The eliminated small molecule is hydrogen bromide in effect, though OH- and Br- carry the charges.

low.restatement: Ethanolic conditions plus heat push the hydroxide's role from nucleophile to base: it removes hydrogen, the C-X pair leaves as X-, and the liberated electrons close into the new double bond.
low.analogy: A tug-of-war where the base pulls one end (H), the halogen keeps its electron pair, and the chain snaps taut into a double bond.
low.examPointer: Contrast with the aqueous route explicitly - same reagent, different solvent, different class of product: alkene not alcohol.

medium.restatement: The elimination follows an E2-style concert: C-H and C-X bonds reorganise in one step, ejecting halide and building the pi bond. Heterolytic C-X breaking hands both electrons to the halogen as X-.
medium.analogy: A spreadsheet row deleted in one action: hydrogens and halogen leave together, and the freed electrons redraw the row as a double line.
medium.examPointer: Write the products as alkene + X- + water (with OH- consumed as base), and name the C-X fission heterolytic.

check.stem: The conditions for the alkene route are

options.explanation: Ethanol solvent plus heat selects the elimination pathway.
Aqueous conditions give substitution to the alcohol.
That gives the nitrile substitution.
Water hydrolyses too slowly and stays on the substitution track.

check.stem: In the elimination, the C-X bond breaks

options.text: Heterolytically, both electrons leaving with the halogen as X-
options.explanation: The pair departs with the electronegative halogen.

options.text: Homolytically, one electron to carbon and one to halogen
options.explanation: No radicals form in this route.

options.text: Not at all, as X- stays bonded
options.explanation: The halogen leaves as an ion.
Hydroxide takes hydrogen, not the C-X electrons.

check.stem: Bromoethane heated with ethanolic NaOH gives

options.explanation: The elimination installs the double bond on the two-carbon chain.
That is the aqueous route's product.
No cyanide is present.
No ammonia is present.

check.stem: The role of hydroxide in the elimination route is best described as

options.text: A base removing hydrogen so the double bond can form
options.explanation: The base's proton-abstraction role, not its nucleophilic one, dominates in ethanol.
That is the aqueous-route role.
Ethanol is the solvent.
Hydroxide is consumed to water.

check.stem: Why does changing the solvent from water to ethanol flip substitution into elimination?

options.text: Solvation and conditions change the balance of pathways, favouring H removal over lone-pair attack
options.explanation: The medium tunes which role of OH- wins.

options.text: Ethanol reacts directly with the halogenoalkane
options.explanation: Ethanol is the solvent, not a reactant here.
Water supports substitution readily.

options.text: The halogen behaves differently in ethanol
options.explanation: The substrate is unchanged; the pathway balance shifts.

check.stem: State the products when a halogenoalkane undergoes ethanolic elimination.
check.modelAnswer: An alkene plus halide ion (X-) - the C-X bond breaks heterolytically.

check.stem: State the elimination product from bromoethane.
check.modelAnswer: Ethene, the two-carbon alkene carrying the new double bond.

check.stem: Explain why heating is required for the elimination route.
check.modelAnswer: Elimination has a higher energetic demand than substitution, so sustained heating under the ethanolic conditions drives the pathway.

check.stem: Predict the product of 2-bromopropane with hot ethanolic NaOH and state what happens to the C-Br bond.
check.modelAnswer: Propene forms; the C-Br bond breaks heterolytically, the electron pair leaving with bromide while the freed electrons build the C=C.

glossary.definition: An electron-rich species donating an electron pair to an electron-deficient carbon.
The splitting of a molecule by reaction with water; the aqueous alkali route is the fast version of it.
Continuous boiling-and-condensing that sustains heating without losing volatile reagents.
The removal of a small molecule (effectively HX) from a halogenoalkane to leave an alkene.
